analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent the 2003 capital gains and dividend tax cuts, cuts individual and corporate income tax rates, and trims domestic spending.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced with 87 Republican cosponsors in the Democratic-controlled House on January 13, 2009, it was sent to two committees and died there when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make the 2003 reductions in capital gains and dividend tax rates permanent, cut every individual income tax rate by 5% of its value, cut the top corporate rate from 35% to 25%, and repeal the individual alternative minimum tax. It would also raise the child tax credit to $5,000, allow tax-free IRA withdrawals in 2009, increase tuition and student-loan-interest deductions, and boost business tax breaks like expensing and a 7-year loss carryback. To pay for a small slice of it, it cuts 1% from every non-defense domestic program for fiscal 2009; the rest would add to the deficit.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations and investors gain the most: a 25% top corporate rate, a 15% corporate capital gains rate, a permanent research credit, unlimited expensing of equipment, and a 7-year loss carryback. Higher-income households gain from permanent 15% dividend and capital gains rates, inflation indexing of gains, and AMT repeal. Middle-income families get smaller, real benefits: a 5% cut in their rates, a $5,000 (but nonrefundable) child credit, tax-free 2009 IRA withdrawals, and larger tuition and student-loan-interest deductions.

how_it_helps.text: Makes permanent the 15% tax rates on capital gains and dividends enacted in 2003, which were otherwise scheduled to expire after 2010.
Cuts each individual income tax rate by 5% (for example, the 25% rate falls to 23.75%) and repeals the individual alternative minimum tax.
Cuts the top corporate income tax rate from 35% to 25% and the corporate capital gains rate from 35% to 15%.
Raises the child tax credit from $1,000 to $5,000, though the credit would remain nonrefundable, so families owing little income tax get nothing from the increase.
Excludes 2009 IRA withdrawals from income and ends required minimum distributions from IRAs after 2009.
Increases the tuition deduction to as much as $6,000 and the student-loan-interest deduction to $3,750, with higher income limits.

Makes the research credit permanent, allows a 7-year carryback of business losses, repeals dollar limits on expensing of business equipment, and lets investors adjust the basis of assets for inflation.

analysis.who_pays: The bill contains no offsetting revenue; the rate cuts, AMT repeal, and business provisions would be financed by borrowing, adding to the national debt. Every non-defense domestic program — education, housing, transit, research, and more — would lose 1% of its fiscal 2009 funding, while defense and veterans programs are exempt. Families with little income tax liability gain nothing from the enlarged child credit because it is nonrefundable.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Treasury, and domestic program recipients

drawbacks.text: The largest provisions flow to corporations and investors: permanent 15% dividend and capital gains rates, inflation indexing of gains, AMT repeal, and the corporate rate cuts primarily reduce taxes on those with investment income and corporate profits.
The bill has no revenue offsets; it cuts 1% of non-defense domestic spending in fiscal 2009 while the far larger tax cuts are deficit-financed, increasing the national debt.
The $5,000 child tax credit would remain nonrefundable, so the families least able to pay for children's needs — those owing little or no income tax — would get no benefit from the increase.
Repealing the individual AMT without replacing the revenue would primarily benefit upper-income taxpayers, since the AMT largely falls on high earners in high-tax states.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill mixes genuinely useful middle-class tax relief (lower rates, bigger education deductions, tax-free IRA withdrawals) with much larger, permanent benefits for corporations and investors. The costs are real: no revenue offsets, a 1% cut to every non-defense domestic program, and a materially larger long-term deficit, since the 2003 investment-tax cuts would never sunset. The title's 'middle-class' framing describes the smallest parts of the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Appropriations committees on the day it was introduced, neither committee ever acted on it, and it expired when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Scott Garrett of New Jersey, joined by Representatives Tom Price of Georgia and Jim Jordan of Ohio, introduced the bill on January 13, 2009, three days after the new Democratic-controlled Congress convened.
It was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Appropriations Committee, the standard first step for a tax bill.
Eighty-seven of the 178 House Republicans signed on as cosponsors; no Democrat did.
Neither committee scheduled a markup or vote, the House never took up the bill, and it died at the end of the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, corporations and investors did not receive the proposed permanent rate cuts, and fiscal 2009 non-defense domestic programs were not cut by this bill. In a year when Congress instead enacted the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, this proposal simply disappeared with no action by anyone; the majority's decision to ignore it, rather than any recorded vote, decided the outcome.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Domestic programs kept their funding; no new tax cuts

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Republican — all 87 cosponsors were House Republicans, and no Democrat signed on — while the Democratic majority controlling the committees never acted on it.

industries.note: A 25% top corporate rate, a 15% corporate capital gains rate, a permanent research credit, a 7-year loss carryback, and unlimited equipment expensing would sharply cut corporate tax bills. The cost would be borne by the Treasury — and eventually taxpayers — through added debt.

Permanent 15% dividend and capital gains rates, inflation indexing of gains held over three years, and AMT repeal concentrate their benefits on households with large investment income, while the bill's cost lands on the deficit. The nonrefundable child credit increase also skips families with little income tax liability.

industries.industry: Non-defense domestic programs (education, transit, housing, research agencies)
industries.note: A 1% across-the-board rescission would cut every fiscal 2009 non-defense discretionary program, with defense and veterans accounts exempt. These are the programs that fund services ordinary people use directly.
Repealing the dollar limits on expensing of equipment and extending the loss-carryback period would let businesses of all sizes deduct investment immediately and offset income with past losses.
